tldr: This paper reveals the gap between predictive utility and decision utility—physical parameters that help predict deformation do not necessarily help choose manipulation actions—and shows that directly leveraging interaction history as a latent representation achieves the best zero-shot control performance on hardware.
hero_caption: Overview of the framework: (a) Physical simulations with varying stiffness and friction generate (b) three physical-context representations: ground-truth parameters, estimated parameters, and interaction history. (c) These are fed into a forward prediction model and GPF policies, (d) comparing predictive utility versus decision utility, followed by (e) zero-shot transfer to a physical UR5 robot without any real-world training.
overview:
In robotic manipulation of Deformable Linear Objects (DLOs) like cables and wires, pulling an object the same way can lead to drastically different deformed shapes depending on its stiffness and surface friction. The standard approach has long been either identifying physical parameters like Young's modulus and friction coefficient to feed into a policy, or building forward dynamics models that accurately predict deformation.

However, the authors raise a fundamental question: Is the representation that best predicts an object's deformation really the one most useful for deciding how the robot should act? This brings the classic insight of control-oriented system identification—that representations favoring predictive models are not necessarily optimal for control policies—into deep-learning-based deformable object manipulation.

To investigate this, the authors developed Geometry–Pointer–Flow (GPF), a highly efficient policy backbone that decouples grasp-location selection from motion generation. Using this backbone, they prepared three forms of physical context: simulator ground-truth parameters, parameters estimated from interaction history, and learned latent representations directly extracted from history. They then rigorously compared their predictive utility (forward prediction accuracy) and decision utility (executed control performance) in simulation and on a physical robot.

Surprisingly, estimated physical parameters, despite showing high predictive accuracy for deformation, provided no detectable improvement in policy control accuracy. In contrast, a model that learned latent representations directly from interaction history without explicitly reconstructing specific physical quantities reduced policy executed error by about 10% and achieved the highest success rate in zero-shot transfer to a physical robot without any real-world training. This study highlights that what matters most is not cleanly identifying physical parameters, but rather how to represent historical interaction cues directly relevant to action decisions.
contributions: Systematically demonstrated in a DLO manipulation task that predictive utility (usefulness for predicting deformation) and decision utility (usefulness for deciding actions) do not necessarily align for physical context.

Proposed GPF (Geometry–Pointer–Flow), a geometry-grounded policy that decouples grasp candidate selection (Pointer) from planar motion generation conditioned on the chosen grasp (Flow Matching), achieving substantial parameter reduction, faster inference, and higher accuracy compared to existing diffusion policies.

Demonstrated that bypassing explicit physical parameter bottlenecks to learn and inject latent representations from deformation history performs best on tight-tolerance simulation tasks and real-robot zero-shot closed-loop control.

sections.heading: Does Information Useful for Prediction Also Help Action Decision?
sections.summary: In deformable linear object manipulation, objects with the same appearance behave differently depending on physical properties such as stiffness and friction. This section poses the core question of whether physical context useful for predicting deformation is equally useful for selecting actions, outlining the overall study.
sections.details:
Deformable Linear Objects (DLOs) such as wires, cables, and hoses are common in industrial wiring and domestic robotics, yet they remain one of the hardest challenges in manipulation. Even if two DLOs look completely identical, differences in material stiffness (Young's modulus) or surface friction mean that applying the exact same pulling force will result in completely different deformed shapes.

Prior research has largely followed two directions to tackle this challenge: building forward dynamics models that accurately predict deformation, or identifying physical parameters online to feed into a policy. Both rely on "physical context" (information capturing physical response characteristics). Here, the authors ask a fundamental question: Is the information that best predicts deformation truly the best information for the robot's action decisions?

As recognized in control theory under "control-oriented system identification," minimizing prediction error does not automatically translate to better control performance. Therefore, this study clearly distinguishes between "predictive utility" and "decision utility" of physical context, conducting an exhaustive comparison on a planar single-grasp DLO shape control task.

Alongside a geometry-only baseline, they evaluate three physical-context representations: (1) simulator ground-truth parameters (Oracle), (2) parameters identified from past interaction history (Estimated), and (3) task-oriented latent representations learned directly from interaction history without explicit physical parameter bottlenecks (Hist). These are incorporated into their novel, highly efficient Geometry–Pointer–Flow (GPF) policy backbone and forward prediction models, and tested across both simulation and real-robot zero-shot settings.

captions.F1: Conceptual overview of the study. From identical simulator-generated data, three physical contexts—ground-truth, estimated, and learned latent history—are formed, and their effects are independently evaluated on both forward prediction models and control policies.

sections.heading: Trends in Deformable Manipulation, Structured Policies, and Adaptation
sections.summary: This section reviews prior work on DLO dynamics learning and direct policy learning, positioning the proposed grasp-motion decoupled architecture and physical adaptation mechanism within the broader literature.
sections.details:
Related work is broadly grouped into three categories:

### II-A DLO Manipulation and Dynamics Learning
In deformable linear object manipulation, many model-based control approaches have directly learned deformation dynamics using local linear models, graph neural networks, or differentiable state-space models. While capable of predicting physical responses, they do not answer whether the learned predictive model is optimal for decision-making in control policies.

### II-B Structured and Generative Manipulation Policies
In robotic manipulation, structured policies that combine discrete contact location selection with continuous motion generation (such as HACMan) and generative models like Diffusion Policy have evolved rapidly. While diffusion-based approaches have been proposed for DLOs, they suffer from high computational cost and slow inference. The proposed GPF combines contact point selection with Rectified Flow for motion generation, achieving a generative policy that is both highly accurate and remarkably fast.

### II-C Physical Context for Adaptation
To adapt to environmental variations, online system identification approaches that feed estimated physical parameters to a policy, as well as methods that infer latent variables from past interaction history (such as RMA: Rapid Motor Adaptation), have demonstrated success in quadrupedal locomotion and grasping. In deformable manipulation, studies have estimated compliance for insertion tasks; however, no prior work has isolated and compared explicit physical parameter identification versus latent history representations under identical conditions for both prediction and control.

sections.heading: Designing Physical Context Representations and the GPF Policy
sections.summary: This section details the formulation of DLO shape control, the extraction and learning of the three physical-context representations, and the architecture of the GPF policy—which decouples grasp selection from flow generation—alongside the forward deformation prediction model.
sections.details:
### III-A Problem Formulation
The setup considers planar manipulation where a single gripper grasps and moves a tabletop DLO in a single step to match a target shape. The current centerline is represented by $n=51$ planar node coordinates $s_t$, and the target shape $g$ is represented similarly. The robot action $a_t$ is a hybrid representation consisting of a discrete index $\alpha_t$ choosing one of $m=24$ candidate grasp segments uniformly distributed along the centerline, and a continuous planar displacement and rotation $(\Delta x_t, \Delta y_t, \Delta \theta_t)$ after grasping.

### III-B Physical-Context Representations
Three physical contexts $c_t$ are compared:
- **Oracle**: True Young's modulus $E$ and friction coefficient $\mu$ obtained directly from the simulator.
- **Estimated**: $(\hat{E}_t, \hat{\mu}_t)$ identified using a pretrained, frozen Transformer from up to 5 steps of recent interaction history (pre-action centerline, chosen grasp, executed action, post-action centerline).
- **Hist**: Using the exact same 5-step history as input, bypasses explicit physical parameter bottlenecks to learn a 32-dimensional task-oriented latent vector $z_t$ via a 1D-CNN and temporal attention. An auxiliary loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{aux}}$ predicting $E, \mu$ is added during training for regularization, but the encoder is trained jointly end-to-end with the downstream model (predictor or policy).

### III-C Geometry–Pointer–Flow Manipulation Policy (GPF)
GPF decouples "where to grasp" from "how to move the selected point":
1. **Geometry Encoder**: Encodes current and target node features jointly with a Transformer to extract grasp candidate features and a global feature.
2. **Grasp Selection (Pointer)**: Computes grasp scores via dot-product attention using the global feature as query and grasp segment features as keys to classify the optimal grasp $\alpha_t$.
3. **Motion Generation (Rectified Flow)**: Concatenates local features of the selected grasp with the global feature as conditioning, generating continuous action vector $u_t$ from noise via a conditional Rectified Flow over 10 Euler integration steps.
4. **Context Injection**: Physical context $c_t$ is injected either via direct concatenation with grasp queries and motion generation conditioning, or via FiLM (Feature-wise Linear Modulation) scaling and shifting geometric features (Hist-FiLM).

### III-D Forward-Response Prediction
A forward prediction model evaluates predictive utility. Without access to the target shape $g$, it takes the current shape $s_t$, executed action $a_t$, and physical context $c_t$ to predict post-execution node displacements $\Delta p_{t+1}$. It is trained completely independently from the policies.

captions.F2: State and action representations for planar single-grasp DLO manipulation. One candidate segment along the centerline point sequence is chosen as the grasp point, and translation $(\Delta x_t, \Delta y_t)$ and rotation $\Delta \theta_t$ from that point are determined simultaneously to align with the target shape (dashed line).

sections.heading: Physics Simulator Environment and Real-Robot Zero-Shot Setup
sections.summary: This section describes the large-scale data generation and evaluation protocol using the AGX Dynamics simulator, as well as the setup for zero-shot transfer to a physical UR5 robot without any real-world training.
sections.details:
### IV-A Dataset and Simulation
The high-fidelity AGX Dynamics simulator is used. A 0.5 m cable is modeled with 24 constrained segments and resampled into a 51-node centerline. Young's modulus $E \in [20, 200]\,\mathrm{kPa}$ (log-uniform) and surface friction coefficient $\mu \in [0.15, 0.60]$ (uniform) are varied randomly, yielding a dataset of 90,106 episodes (approximately 900,000 transitions). Physical properties are fixed per episode, where reachable shapes are generated by settling random initial configurations and applying feasible actions.

### IV-B Manipulation Policy Baselines
To evaluate GPF, several baselines are compared:
- **MLP-BC / Transformer-BC**: Behavioral cloning directly regressing actions from geometric inputs.
- **Global-Flow**: Flow matching conditioned only on global features without local grasp conditioning.
- **GPF-Geom**: The proposed geometry-only baseline without physical context.
- **DLO-DP**: A DLO-specific Diffusion Policy based on prior work, using 100-step DDPM to generate action trajectories.

### IV-C Evaluation Protocol
Control performance is measured by the mean distance between post-execution centerline nodes and target nodes (mean node shape error, in mm). Inference latency is measured on an RTX 2080 Ti with batch size 1. Statistical significance is assessed with 95% confidence intervals from 5,000 bootstrap resamples.

### IV-D Real-Robot Evaluation
The real-world setup consists of a UR5 robot, a Robotiq Hand-E gripper, and a wrist-mounted OAK camera. Although a Franka Emika Panda was used in simulation, actions are defined in DLO-centric relative coordinates, requiring no policy modifications across different robot arms or grippers.
Real-world experiments evaluate six conditions combining three cable stiffnesses (Soft, Medium, Stiff) and two surface types (a rough cork board and a smooth cloth-covered surface). Models trained exclusively in simulation are evaluated directly via complete zero-shot transfer, without any real-world training or fine-tuning.

sections.heading: The Divergence Between Prediction and Control, and Real-Robot Performance
sections.summary: Results show that GPF achieves substantially faster inference and higher accuracy than existing diffusion models, predictive accuracy rankings invert when applied to control in simulation, and the interaction history model achieves the best closed-loop performance on the physical robot.
sections.details:
### V-A GPF Architecture Evaluation
Comparing geometry-only policies, the proposed GPF-Geom reduced one-step executed shape error by 32.8% relative to the prior DLO-DP (diffusion policy). Furthermore, it achieved this with 18.7 $\times$ fewer parameters and approximately 193 $\times$ faster inference (2.52 ms for GPF vs. 486 ms for DLO-DP). Explicitly decoupling "where to grasp" from "how to move" proves highly effective.

### V-B Predictive Utility of Physical Context
In simulation forward deformation prediction, ground-truth parameters (Oracle) achieved the highest accuracy, reducing error by 2.391 mm over geometry alone (None). Estimated parameters (Estimated) followed, outperforming learned latent representations (Hist) by 0.146 mm (95% CI $[0.095, 0.198]$). For the task of predicting deformation, explicit parameter identification proved superior to latent representations.
However, across 1,800 real-robot transitions, this ordering inverted: Hist achieved the lowest prediction error, while Estimated—which performed well in simulation—degraded to worse than geometry alone (None). The sim-to-real gap degraded the parameter estimator itself.

### V-C Decision Utility in Executed Manipulation
This is the central highlight of the paper. Comparing one-step control performance in simulation, Estimated (which beat Hist in prediction) showed no statistically detectable control improvement over geometry alone (GPF-Geom), with its confidence interval crossing zero. Meanwhile, Hist-FiLM reduced executed error by 9.9% (0.852 mm improvement) over GPF-Geom, clearly outperforming Estimated.
This directly confirms the divergence: the physical context most effective for forward prediction is not the context most effective for action decision.

### V-D Closed-Loop Manipulation
This advantage persisted in closed-loop control over up to 10 steps:
- **Simulation**: At a strict 5 mm tolerance, Hist-FiLM achieved a 36% success rate, significantly ahead of GPF-Geom (25%) and DLO-DP (20%).
- **Physical Robot**: Across 60 rollouts, Hist-FiLM attained the lowest mean and median shape errors, as well as the highest 10 mm attainment rate. It improved best-in-rollout error by 1.28 mm over GPF-Geom, demonstrating superior zero-shot adaptation.

captions.F5: Zero-shot closed-loop manipulation with GPF Hist-FiLM on the physical robot. Across three different stiffness and surface conditions, large initial shape errors at step 0 smoothly converge to within a few millimeters by steps 3 and 10.

sections.heading: Why Do Prediction and Decision Utilities Diverge?
sections.summary: This section examines why physical parameter identification failed to improve control while history representations excelled on hardware, and discusses the limitations of the experimental setup and directions for future work.
sections.details:
Why did estimated parameters $(\hat{E}, \hat{\mu})$, despite helping deformation prediction, fail to enhance control, while the latent history representation (Hist) proved so powerful? The authors consider several reasons.

First, compressing information into simplified physical parameters like Young's modulus and friction coefficient creates an informational bottleneck that can discard local stress variations and complex contact histories—details critical for deciding the next control action. Because Hist is not constrained to specific physical parameters, it can flexibly retain information directly tied to task completion from recent deformation responses. Indeed, shuffling historical correspondences severely degraded Hist's performance, confirming that it actively leverages step-by-step deformation feedback.

Second, Hist's standout performance in zero-shot transfer stems from its robustness to the sim-to-real gap. While explicit parameter estimators degraded significantly due to contact discrepancies between simulation and reality, the end-to-end latent representation helped correct subtle discrepancies that geometry alone could not account for.

Nonetheless, the paper notes several limitations:
- The exact physical and task features embedded within the Hist latent space are not yet fully understood.
- Because physical experiments require manual resets, perfectly paired rollouts starting from identical initial configurations across controllers are inherently impossible on hardware.
- The impact of physical context also varied across policy backbones (GPF vs. Diffusion Policy), leaving the causal interaction between network architecture and context integration not fully decoupled.

sections.heading: Physical Context Should Be Evaluated by Decision Quality, Not Predictive Accuracy
sections.summary: The paper concludes by reiterating that the quality of physical context should be judged not by how accurately it predicts forward dynamics, but by the quality of the decisions it enables.
sections.details:
This study demonstrates that in deformable linear object manipulation, the physical representation most useful for predicting deformation is not necessarily the one most useful for deciding manipulation actions.

The proposed GPF policy established a strong baseline, outperforming existing diffusion-based policies in accuracy while running approximately 193 $\times$ faster. On top of this backbone, latent representations learned from recent interaction history proved far more effective than explicit parameter estimation for high-precision simulation control and real-robot zero-shot transfer.

For future work in deformable manipulation and robot learning, this offers a crucial takeaway: when designing physical context or world models, representations should not be judged merely because they reduce forward prediction error. Instead, evaluation must be grounded in decision utility—how much they ultimately improve the robot's action choices.

takeaways: Accurate world models do not guarantee superior control: forward deformation prediction accuracy does not directly correlate with a policy's ability to choose effective actions, making direct evaluation on control tasks essential.

Pitfalls of explicit parameter identification: compressing observations into classical parameters like Young's modulus or friction discards task-relevant history and risks estimator breakdown during real-world transfer.

Decoupling grasp selection and motion generation (Where/How decomposition): separating contact selection from trajectory generation, as in GPF, yields policies an order of magnitude smaller and nearly two orders of magnitude faster than diffusion policies.

Power of latent history representations in zero-shot adaptation: an interaction history encoder trained purely in simulation provides strong zero-shot adaptation to unseen stiffness and friction on physical hardware without fine-tuning.
limitations: What specific physical features are captured in the latent representation (Hist) remains largely a black box without full causal interpretability.
Due to manual resets in physical robot experiments, perfectly paired evaluations from identical initial states (as done in simulation) are impossible on hardware.
The task is limited to planar single-gripper DLO shape control; extension to 3D knotting, dynamic manipulation, or multi-fingered grasping remains unverified.
